sub_answers.sub_question: Known limitations of SDP relaxations, including relaxation gap and infeasible rank conditions
sub_answers.text: SDP relaxations can be inexact and exhibit a positive optimality gap even on very small radial-network examples, with outcomes that include exactness, inexactness, or feasibility of the relaxation while the original problem is infeasible [d24659s0p0]. The exactness of an SDP relaxation is closely tied to rank-one generation properties of the feasible PSD cone intersection; lacking those properties prevents guaranteed rank-one (exact) solutions [d60142s0p0]. Comparisons in power-flow applications show SDP relaxations are not universally dominating: the QC relaxation is stronger than SOC and neither dominates nor is dominated by SDP, so SDP can be weaker or stronger depending on problem structure [d26453s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Nonconvexity, local minima, and global optimality issues associated with QCQP formulations
sub_answers.text: Quadratically constrained quadratic programs are nonconvex and can have many complex critical points, with the coordinates of optimizers being algebraic functions of input coefficients and a computable algebraic degree that reflects this multiplicity [d2055s0p0]. The nonconvexity and discontinuities that arise in sparse QCQP settings require specialized stationarity concepts and reformulations to derive meaningful first- and second-order optimality conditions [d80058s0p0]. Algorithmic approaches for QCQP exploit these optimality structures (e.g., P-stationarity and semismooth Newton methods) to obtain locally fast convergence, indicating the central practical challenge is escaping non-global stationary points to reach global optima [d106579s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Numerical stability and sensitivity to modeling errors for constrained least squares in radar
Trade-offs between model fidelity and computational tractability in choosing SDP versus QCQP
sub_answers.text: Using stronger relaxations or formulations (e.g., SDP) can improve model fidelity but often incurs higher computational cost and solver reliability issues compared to lighter relaxations; QC and SOC relaxations are reported to be significantly faster and more reliable than current SDP solvers in power-flow experiments [d26453s0p0]. The QC relaxation preserves stronger links between voltage variables via convex envelopes in polar form and can produce substantial accuracy improvements over SOC at reasonable computational cost, representing a middle ground between fidelity and tractability [d26453s0p0]. In other application domains, non-SDP methods (e.g., manifold optimization) can outperform multiple SDP-based benchmarks both in solution quality and computational complexity, illustrating practical trade-offs favoring non-SDP approaches when solver cost or scalability is critical [d76687s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Debates in the literature regarding robustness of optimization-based waveform design to clutter and interference
How waveform design constraints (power, PAPR, spectral mask) are implemented in optimization formulations
sub_answers.text: Spectral and PAPR constraints are enforced as explicit constraints in the optimization problem (e.g., maximize PSLR subject to spectral mask and PAPR limits) [d81182s0p0]. The peak and average power constraints are modeled directly in information-theoretic formulations and can be expressed via a PAPR parameter A in low-SNR capacity scaling results [d43534s0p0]. Optimization formulations therefore incorporate these requirements as hard constraints or parameters that restrict feasible waveform amplitudes and spectra during design [d81182s0p0][d43534s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Impact of problem size on real-time implementability of SDP and QCQP in radar systems
sub_answers.text: Semidefinite programs (SDPs) and large QCQPs face significant computational burdens as problem dimension grows, which limits real-time implementability for large-scale systems [d88612s0p0]. Exploiting problem structure or symmetry can dramatically reduce search-space dimensionality and computational complexity, improving feasibility for near-real-time use [d88612s0p0]. Under certain conditions SDP relaxations become tight and solvable in polynomial time, which can make them more practical if problem size and structure permit [d61455s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Typical performance metrics used to evaluate joint receiver and waveform design (SINR, detection probability)
sub_answers.text: Waveform/receiver joint designs are evaluated with metrics such as sidelobe level (SLCL) and peak side lobe ratio (PSLR) for correlation performance [d81182s0p0]. Mean-square error (weighted sum-MSE or max weighted MSE) is a common metric for transceiver optimization performance [d21050s0p0]. Error-rate and detection-related metrics like symbol error rate (SER), signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR), and system energy-efficiency or transmit power minimization are also used depending on objective (e.g., CE precoding and IRS-NOMA studies) [d32544s0p0][d76687s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Hardware and execution-time considerations when implementing optimization-based radar processing
sub_answers.text: Hardware choices such as constant-envelope transmission enable highly efficient power amplification and can reduce RF-chain complexity (e.g., single RF chain CE precoding) which eases hardware implementation of optimized waveforms [d32544s0p0]. Algorithmic complexity directly affects execution time, and lower-complexity manifold or structure-exploiting methods can yield much lower computational cost than SDP-based benchmarks, reducing run-time requirements [d76687s0p0][d88612s0p0]. When SDP relaxations are tight and solvable efficiently, they become viable, but otherwise hardware/real-time constraints favor lower-complexity reformulations or approximations [d61455s0p0][d88612s0p0].

Typical convexity properties of constrained least squares, SDP, and QCQP
sub_answers.text: Constrained least squares problems can lead to symmetric positive definite systems under appropriate stabilization, implying convexity of the least-squares objective in those settings [d71424s0p0]. Semidefinite programs (SDPs) form a convex optimization class widely used for relaxations and large-scale problems in data science and signal processing [d55114s0p0]. Quadratically constrained quadratic programs (QCQPs) are generally nonconvex and computationally challenging, and are often relaxed to SDPs to obtain tractable solutions [d61455s0p0][d106579s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Common numerical algorithms used to solve constrained least squares problems
sub_answers.text: Krylov subspace projection methods (e.g., Golub–Kahan bidiagonalization) are used to reduce large constrained least squares problems to smaller projected problems solved iteratively [d100164s0p0]. Hybrid schemes combine Krylov projection with regularization and inner LSQR solves, improving conditioning and convergence of the inner least squares problems [d100164s0p0]. Krylov-based iterative methods can be adapted to least squares with linear equality constraints by decomposing the solution into operator-form components and approximating each via Krylov subspaces [d103964s0p0]. Deterministic sketching approaches (recursive importance sketching) solve rank-constrained least squares by solving dimension-reduced least squares subproblems with fast local convergence [d63101s0p0]. Randomized numerical linear algebra techniques (e.g., sketching and repeated halving) are applied to large Toeplitz least squares problems to accelerate fitting in big-data time series settings [d72834s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Interior-point and first-order methods for solving semidefinite programs
Typical solution approaches and relaxations for nonconvex QCQPs
sub_answers.text: Nonconvex binary quadratic and related QCQPs are commonly relaxed by spectral methods, which are simple but yield loose bounds [d18288s0p0]. Semidefinite programming relaxations provide tighter bounds for BQPs/QCQPs but are computationally heavier in their conventional formulations [d18288s0p0]. Reformulations of SDP relaxations can enable more efficient and scalable dual optimization approaches that approach the complexity of spectral methods while retaining tighter bounds [d18288s0p0].

Literature documenting cases where semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations for quadratic problems exhibit a nonzero relaxation gap: explicit counterexamples, bounds on the gap magnitude, and necessary/sufficient rank conditions (e.g., when the relaxation fails to produce a rank-1 solution); references proving when rank constraints become infeasible and methods to detect or certify infeasibility.
sub_answers.text: Specific small explicit counterexamples and a complete characterization of when the SDP relaxation has a positive optimality gap are given for optimal power flow over radial networks, including a two-bus one-generator system where the relaxation can be exact, inexact, or feasible while the original problem is infeasible, and a library of such instances is provided [d24659s0p0]. Sufficient and (in some cases) necessary structural conditions that guarantee rank-one (exact) solutions are studied via the rank-one generated (ROG) cone framework, which links extreme rays generated by rank-one matrices to exactness of SDP relaxations and gives verifiable sufficient conditions and necessity results for the two-LMI case [d60142s0p0]. Constructive algebraic reformulations can produce exact infeasibility certificates and yield algorithms that generate constraints of all infeasible SDPs and all feasible SDPs with a fixed-rank maximal solution, providing tools to detect or certify infeasibility and rank-related properties [d23484s0p0]. There are instances and relaxation constructions showing exactness for small numbers of constraints (e.g., polynomial-size SDP relaxations exact for m=1 and m=2 in certain quadratic problems) but lack of a general explicit tractable exact representation for higher m, demonstrating limits on when rank-1 reconstruction can be guaranteed [d83454s0p0].

In waveform optimization problems for radar, how are constraints such as total transmit power, per-antenna/element power limits, peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) caps, and spectral emission masks modeled mathematically (e.g., quadratic constraints, norm bounds, spectral shaping constraints), and how are those implemented in concrete optimization formulations (SDP relaxations, convex approximations, penalty terms)?
sub_answers.text: Per-antenna and per-element transmit-power limits and PAPR caps are imposed as convex constraints on the precoded/waveform entries, e.g., explicit bounds on the magnitude of each symbol/antenna element or norm bounds on the transmit vector entries [d76411s0p0][d81182s0p0]. Quadratic constraints and QCQP formulations are used when power or waveform-energy terms appear quadratically, and nonconvex waveform constraints are often handled by manifold-optimization or alternating-optimization approaches [d70545s0p0][d65110s0p0]. SDP relaxations and SOCP (second-order cone) or QC relaxations are commonly used to convexify or approximate nonconvex QCQPs, with SDP/SOCP/QC relaxations trading off tightness and solver cost [d26453s0p0][d70545s0p0]. Penalty-term approaches and exact-penalty reformulations (turning constrained problems into unconstrained ones) and smoothing techniques are used to handle hard constraints such as phase-only or feasibility expansion problems on manifolds [d76687s0p0][d65110s0p0].

What specific objective and evaluation metrics are most commonly used to judge joint transmit waveform and receiver filter designs (e.g., output SINR, detection probability/ROC curves under Swerling target models, false-alarm rate, Cramér–Rao lower bound on parameter estimation, clutter/interference suppression ratio), and how are these metrics estimated in simulations or measured in experiments?
sub_answers.text: Output SINR (or SINR-maximization) is a primary objective used to judge joint transmit waveform and receive filter designs [d65110s0p0]. Detection-related metrics such as bit-error probability or SINAD, and measures of per-user or per-target distortion/power, are used in communications-oriented or precoding analyses [d76411s0p0]. Waveform-specific metrics like peak-sidelobe level (SLCL) and peak sidelobe ratio (PSLR) under spectral and PAPR constraints are used in OFDM and radar sequence design studies [d81182s0p0]. Deliverable power and end-to-end efficiency are used in beamforming and power-transfer contexts and evaluated via numerical results or simulations [d29185s0p0][d76687s0p0].

List and compare specific numerical algorithms and implementations used to solve least-squares problems with equality, inequality, or bound constraints (e.g., constrained QR/LSQR, augmented-Lagrangian methods, projected/conjugate-gradient variants, active-set solvers, trust-region approaches), noting when each is preferred and key stability/complexity trade-offs.
sub_answers.text: Krylov-subspace projection methods (hybrid LSMR) project A onto a Krylov subspace via Golub–Kahan bidiagonalization and solve regularized inner least-squares with LSQR, which is preferred for very large, ill-conditioned or matrix-free LSE problems because it avoids dense factorizations and inner LSQR becomes better conditioned as iteration k grows [d100164s0p0][d103964s0p0]. Orthogonal projection onto constraint nullspaces can be implemented by sparse QR factorization or by a preconditioned LSQR iteration, trading the robustness of factorization for the memory and arithmetic savings of iterative solves when C is sparse [d64743s0p0]. Augmented Lagrangian methods modified to incorporate second-order information with an active-set strategy (e.g., an ALGENCAN variant) are used when stronger convergence and robustness are required and when second-order models are affordable; they bring asymptotic quadratic convergence at the cost of Hessian/linear-system work per iteration [d67089s0p0]. Projected quasi-Newton or projected BFGS within trust-region frameworks solve constrained trust-region subproblems efficiently (often in a low-dimensional subspace) and are preferred when one can exploit curvature cheaply and maintain feasibility via projections, yielding faster local convergence but requiring management of projections and possibly expensive subproblem solves [d59387s0p0][d82955s0p0]. For large structured convex QP-like problems one can use two-phase proximal augmented Lagrangian schemes (QPPAL) that warm-start then refine with a proximal AL method to trade a cheaper Phase I for a more expensive high-accuracy Phase II, which improves scalability on high-dimensional convex quadratic programs with many constraints [d66150s0p0].

sub_answers.text: Quadratic Convex (QC) relaxations can produce significantly better accuracy than Second-Order Cone (SOC) relaxations while remaining at a reasonable computational cost, and the QC relaxation is stronger than SOC but neither dominates nor is dominated by the SDP relaxation [d26453s0p0]. QC and SOC relaxations are reported to be substantially faster and more reliable than SDP relaxations with current solvers, indicating a runtime and robustness advantage for lower-fidelity relaxations in many practical cases [d26453s0p0]. Entropy-penalized SDP variants claim an efficient numerical algorithm with (almost) linear-time gradient iterations, offering a practical trade-off of promoting low-rank solutions while substantially reducing per-iteration cost compared to standard SDP solvers [d42341s0p0].
